item.title: AgenticVMD
item.description:
Overview

A natural language interface for VMD (Visual Molecular Dynamics). Provide a PDB file or RCSB PDB ID, describe a visualization in plain English, and get a rendered image.

VMD is a powerful tool for visualizing and analyzing molecular structures, but generating the Tcl scripts it requires can be a steep barrier as it is not a common scripting language even among computational scientists. AgenticVMD removes that barrier by letting users describe what they want to see and handling the translation automatically and you can also edit the TCL script and use it yourself.

item.title: Binding Affinity ML
item.description:
Overview

One of the most important — and expensive — questions in drug discovery is: does this molecule actually stick to its target? When a drug works, a small molecule fits snugly into a protein and disrupts or activates it. The strength of that fit is called binding affinity, measured as pKd — the higher the number, the tighter the grip.

Running experiments to measure binding affinity for thousands of drug candidates is slow and costly. This project explores how well a machine learning model can predict it directly from the 3D structure of a protein–ligand complex.

item.title: Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations for HBV
item.description:
The question

How does drug binding change the way viral proteins assemble into a capsid? This project studies Hepatitis B virus assembly with coarse-grained kinetic Monte Carlo simulations.

My contribution

I extended a C++ kinetic Monte Carlo framework to model drug-binding effects on assembly. I used Markov State Models to analyze assembly pathways and kinetics, connecting simulated trajectories to interpretable descriptions of how the system evolves.

Why it matters

Understanding assembly means looking beyond a completed structure to the pathways that produce it. These computational models complement in vitro experiments by helping investigate how molecular interactions change the process.

item.title: Elastic Network Model for HBV Assembly
item.description:
The question

How can we study the mechanics of viral assembly without tracking every atom? My work uses a coarse-grained elastic network model to represent the interactions and flexibility of Hepatitis B virus proteins.

My approach

I developed the model using OpenMM and NAMD, with parameters learned from all-atom simulation data. The goal is to retain the structural and dynamical behavior relevant to assembly while making larger-scale simulations more tractable.
